items: Two Serbian opposition figures, Vladan Djokic and Rade Bajic, were targeted with cyberespionage tools, including the Pegasus spyware, ahead of Serbia's parliamentary elections.
Citizen Lab and the Share Foundation reported that Djokic's iPhone was hacked, while Bajic received a warning from Apple about potential spyware targeting his phone.
Both men have faced pressure from authorities due to their opposition to the ruling party, with Bajic linking the spyware attack to his involvement in prosecuting government officials.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

Two Serbian opposition figures were recently targeted with powerful cyberespionage tools, according to one of the men and a report issued on Monday, October 19, by the Canadian cyber watchdog group Citizen Lab.

The incident was the latest of several in which researchers say surveillance technology was used against students, opposition politicians, and others in Serbia, which will hold a parliamentary election on Sunday.

Citizen Lab said on Monday that a joint investigation with the Share Foundation, a digital rights group, determined that Serbian academic Vladan Djokic’s iPhone had been hacked using the Pegasus spyware tool made by Israeli group NSO.

At the same time, former prosecutor Rade Bajic told Reuters he received a warning from Apple on August 13 that his phone had been targeted using “mercenary spyware,” although he and Citizen Lab both said they had been unable to establish with certainty whether he was hacked or how a hack might have happened.

Serbia’s Interior Ministry did not return messages seeking comment. Officials there have previously dismissed allegations of cyberespionage. NSO, which was blacklisted by the US government in 2021 following years of reports of alleged human rights abuses, did not return emails. NSO, which says it only sells to governments, has previously said it would terminate commercial relationships that result in serious wrongdoing.
Apple confirmed having sent a batch of warnings to users on August 13 but did not directly address questions about Bajic’s or Djokic’s cases.
Both men have crossed Serbia’s ruling party, which has been buffeted by two years of student-led anti-corruption protests.

Djokic, the rector of the University of Belgrade, has been under pressure from authorities following his expressions of solidarity with the students. About 20 minutes before this story was published, a pro-government tabloid published an article describing Djokic as a “vulture” and purporting to carry audio of him talking about his political ambitions.

The source of the audio was not explained. Djokic said in a statement that the hacking of his phone “points to a serious attack on my privacy, security, and the integrity of the office of Rector” and called for those behind it to be punished. The statement did not address the article and he did not immediately return an email seeking comment about it.

Bajic said he was involved in prosecuting senior government officials over allegations that they improperly removed cultural protections on a historic Belgrade army compound that an investment company founded by US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner, had planned to redevelop. Kushner’s company pulled out of the plan late last year, saying it was doing so out of respect for the people of Serbia and the city of Belgrade.
“In my opinion, my involvement in this case was the sole reason for this unlawful spyware attack,” Bajic said.

Last month, the Share Foundation said that at least 14 people, including students, activists and opposition party members, had been targeted with advanced spyware ahead of local ​elections in March. At least one of the devices was compromised using Pegasus, it said. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Sara Duterte says gov't shifting strategy to take her down
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte on Tuesday claimed that the government is shifting its narratives to bring her down, citing recent reports of the foiled attempt to smuggle illegal drugs from Laos to…

blocks.text: Published October 20, 2026 5:32pm

Vice President Sara Duterte on Tuesday claimed that the government is shifting its narratives to bring her down, citing recent reports of the foiled attempt to smuggle illegal drugs from Laos to Mindanao.

This developed after Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla said in a Palace briefing that former Bangsamoro Parliament member Edriezan Hadji Nasser Rimbang, the Mindanao politician allegedly involved in the attempted smuggling of P3.5 billion worth of shabu from Laos to the Philippines, was in the same political party as former president Rodrigo Duterte.
Remulla later clarified that the Duterte family has no links to the foiled attempt to smuggle the 521 kilograms of illegal drugs.
The vice president, in return, said no evidence has been presented regarding such a "conspiracy."

"Now, we are witnessing an apparent shift in the government's narrative in taking me down, attempting to reframe the matter as a national security issue. Every thread seems to be stretched into a conspiracy—from a business venture allegedly linked to Chinese funding to a drug bust in Laos supposedly connected to a Mindanao-Davao conspiracy," Duterte said in a statement.
"But what evidence does the government have to substantiate these sweeping accusations? None that has been convincingly presented," she added.
The vice president also accused the government of becoming "desperate" in taking her down, given the circulation of an alleged travel authority for Laos.
"What we see instead is desperation, exemplified by a purported travel authority for Laos that appears to have been fabricated to prop up a narrative unsupported by credible evidence," Duterte said.
"Remarkably, the document was never confirmed by the Office of the President on September 29, 2026, who has always made it a point to announce my foreign travels," she continued.
The vice president also reiterated her call for the government to "start working and stop politicking."
GMA News Online has requested comment from Malacañang regarding Duterte's statements, but it has yet to respond as of posting time. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: ‘Disappointed’ Ateneo coach Alas demands maturity from Blue Eagles
articles.summary: ‘I’m super disappointed, but I will not give up on these guys,’ says Ateneo coach Louie Alas after the Blue Eagles’ dismal first-round run

blocks.text: REGROUP. Kieffer Alas (center) and the Blue Eagles huddle on court during UAAP action.
UAAP
‘I’m super disappointed, but I will not give up on these guys,’ says Ateneo coach Louie Alas after the Blue Eagles’ dismal first-round run

items: Ateneo started the UAAP Season 89 men's basketball tournament strong with a 3-1 record but has since lost three consecutive games, leaving them at 3-4 and seventh in the standings.
Head coach Louie Alas expressed disappointment in the team's performance, attributing their struggles to immaturity and a lack of consistency, particularly in the second half of games.
Despite recent losses, Ateneo remains competitive in the league, with the potential to improve in the second round, starting with a home game against FEU.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – Ateneo showed flashes of a contender early in the UAAP Season 89 men’s basketball tournament. Now, head coach Louie Alas wants his Blue Eagles to grow up before their season slips further away.
Ateneo opened the first round with a promising 3-1 record, putting itself among the league’s top teams.
Given the difficult months the program endured following the deaths of student-athletes Divine Adili and Rene Baterbonia, that start was already a significant achievement.
But the Blue Eagles have since lost three straight games, falling to La Salle, FEU and UST, with two of those defeats coming by double-digit margins.
At 3-4 and seventh in the standings, Ateneo finished the first round well below its coach’s expectations.
“I’m disappointed, super disappointed,” Alas said after the Blue Eagles’ 80-68 loss to UST. “My expectations about our record were higher than this.”
Alas pointed to the team’s immaturity, particularly in the second half, when Ateneo has struggled to keep games competitive late in the round.
“Immaturity. It’s immaturity. That’s it,” Alas said. “That’s one thing I really have to improve. We have to become more mature because we are not kids. We have veterans. We are all adults.”
The numbers back up his frustration as Ateneo surrendered at least 80 points in each of its final three games of the first round, while holding opponents below that mark in all three of its wins.
The Blue Eagles allowed the second-most points per game in the league at 81.14, trailing only the winless UE Red Warriors, who gave up 91.71 per contest.

Kieffer Alas, Louie’s 19-year-old son, has led the Blue Eagles with averages of 14.43 points, 4.57 rebounds, 2.43 assists, and 1.57 steals per game. However, he has shot just 34.55% from the field and 20.57% from three-point range.
Jared Bahay has also had difficulty finding his rhythm, averaging 13.0 points, 3.0 rebounds and 4.29 assists while shooting below 40% from the field in the opening round.
His 1-of-13 shooting performance against UST was his worst outing of the first seven games.
Shawn Tuano, Andrew Bongo, Travis Roberts, and Ian Espinosa have likewise struggled to find consistent form, leaving Ateneo searching for more reliable contributions across the roster.
Alas plans to intensify the Blue Eagles’ preparations and practice on top of making the adjustments needed to get them back on track.
“I’m super disappointed, but I will not give up on these guys,” Alas said. “I know they can do a lot better. Maybe we just have to adjust a bit to our practices.”
“I know they can get it right.”
Despite their three-game skid, Ateneo remains within reach of the teams ahead of it in the standings, as a couple of wins to start the second round could quickly change the Blue Eagles’ position.
The Blue Eagles will have home-court advantage to begin the second round when they host the FEU Tamaraws on Saturday, October 24, at the Blue Eagle Gym. – Rappler.com

articles.title: After lower budget in House version, DepEd asks Senate for P147 billion more
articles.summary: The school-based feeding program and ARAL are among the Department of Education programs that may receive higher funding from the Senate

blocks.text: DEPED BUDGET. Education Secretary Sonny Angara presents the proposed 2027 budget of the Department of Education on October 16, 2026.
Department of Education
The school-based feeding program and ARAL are among the Department of Education programs that may receive higher funding from the Senate

items: The Department of Education is requesting an additional P147.93 billion from lawmakers to support its various programs in 2027.
Key funding priorities include nutrition and learning recovery programs.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – With the Senate now focusing on passing its own version of the 2027 budget bill, the Department of Education (DepEd) is seeking support for an additional P147.93 billion to implement its programs next year.

This comes as the DepEd only got P967.23 billion in the House of Representatives’ version of the 2027 general appropriations bill (GAB). This is lower than the P976 billion under the 2027 National Expenditure Program (NEP).

Senator Bam Aquino, who led a budget briefing as chairperson of the Senate finance subcommittee B last Friday, October 16, said his colleagues want an education budget that would reach 4% of the country’s gross domestic product.
Here are some programs that senators may provide higher funding for next year:

Among Aquino’s priorities is putting more money into the DepEd’s school-based feeding program. It has an P11.43-billion allocation in the House’s GAB — the same level in the NEP — but it is significantly lower than the P25.7 billion in the 2026 national budget.
In his presentation, Education Secretary Sonny Angara said the DepEd is seeking P16.82 billion more to at least implement a 180-day feeding cycle for kindergarten and Grade 1.
Senators have a more ambitious move: to provide universal feeding from kindergarten through Grade 3, with a higher unit cost of P30 per meal from the current P25, and a longer cycle of 200 days.
According to DepEd projections, that proposed setup would need an additional P46.65 billion.

blocks.caption: Photo from Department of Education

blocks.text: Aquino had asked for budget scenarios as a bicameral conference committee is set to be convened in the coming weeks for the proposed Expanded National Nutrition Program Act.

“This is one of the biggest reforms that we can do. And if we are able to implement it well, I expect that in three to six years our learning gap problems will be mitigated,” Aquino said in a mix of English and Filipino.
Senators are also expected to inject more funds into the Academic Recovery and Accessible Learning or ARAL Program as part of efforts to address the country’s learning crisis.

blocks.caption: PISA 2025 reality: Nearly 2 in 3 Filipino students are ‘low performers’

blocks.text: During the House deliberations, Angara had pointed out that there was zero funding for the ARAL Program in the NEP. In the House’s GAB, lawmakers only provided P255.6 million for the compensation of external tutors and P94.4 million for program management.
Angara said the DepEd needs P15.63 billion for program implementation next year. Asked for a minimum amount, he cited at least P8.9 billion, or the same level in the 2026 budget.
Senators criticized the Department of Budget and Management (DBM) for not funding the ARAL Program in the first place.
Senate President Win Gatchalian said it was “shocking.” Senator Joel Villanueva called it “stupid.”
Senator Erwin Tulfo said the DBM must review the ARAL Law as it states that funds for the program should be included in the annual General Appropriations Act.

DBM Director Vivien Labastilla explained that while there is no line item for the ARAL Program, funding for it is included in the budget for textbooks and other instructional materials and the DepEd’s basic education curriculum.
Angara maintained it was not. “I think the confusion stems from the fact that they are assuming that it’s already subsumed in our regular budget,” he added.
Aquino also said another priority is funding programs related to school safety, especially since the Senate already passed a bill that institutionalizes a comprehensive school safety framework.
Aside from providing equipment like CCTV camera and metal detectors, the Senate is also eyeing child protection training for parents and student leaders.
The DepEd has a total request of P8.18 billion for school safety and security. The House only provided P500 million to hire security guards.

The full breakdown of the DepEd’s budget request to the Senate is found below. Those highlighted in green are items that were given funding in the House’s GAB, while those in yellow are new appeals or items with a higher requested amount compared to the list previously presented to the House.

blocks.caption: Photo from Department of Education
Photo from Department of Education

blocks.text: Updates on classroom construction are also expected to be tackled in the plenary. During the briefing, the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) reported that there have been failed biddings on their end.

Under the 2026 national budget, around P65.4 billion was allocated to build 18,960 classrooms this year. Of the amount, P21.45 billion was lodged under the agreement between the DPWH and the DepEd to construct 6,000 classrooms.

DPWH Undersecretary Lara Esquibil told senators that only around P1.87 billion, covering the construction of 533 classrooms, have prospective bidders, while the agency is still advertising P7 billion worth of projects, or around 2,000 classrooms.
“They’ve been concerned with the costing of classrooms with fuel price increases,” Esquibil said.
Aquino suggested transferring the remaining funding of nearly P13 billion to the DepEd so that local government units (LGUs) can instead lead the construction projects.
From the target 10,671 classrooms under the LGU-led construction modality, Angara said over 8,000 classrooms are already in the procurement stage.
Aquino will defend the DepEd’s budget in the plenary on November 24. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Why US investors are snapping up Germany's famed Mittelstand
articles.summary: Increasing amounts of US capital are flowing into Germany's traditional industrial firms and family-owned businesses. As many business owners struggle to find successors, more companies are becoming…

image.caption: Traditional German family-owned businesses and SMEs have become increasingly attractive to US companies and investorsImage: Philipp Reinhard/ebm-papst

blocks.text: What do the long-established German companies Birkenstock, Viessmann, Linde and ebm-papst have in common? All have fallen into American hands.
Traditional German family-owned businesses and small-to-medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) have become increasingly attractive to US companies and investors.

Last year, US investors were involved in 76 acquisitions and investments in German industrial and manufacturing companies, according to an analysis by financial data provider PitchBook. The transactions were valued at about $29.5 billion (€26.3 billion) in 2025, nearly double the 2022 total. As of August 19, 2026, the figure stood at $23.9 billion.
No successor, but an investor instead

"From what we are seeing in the market, the interest from US investors in German companies is definitely still there," said Samar-Ahmad Albrecht-Mahmood of Veracity Capital Investments, which advises companies looking to invest in Germany.

German companies, particularly those in the industrial and manufacturing sector, remain attractive, "because many of them are highly specialized, have strong customer relationships and very good technical know-how," he told DW. "In many cases, these are businesses that have built up a strong position in their niche over decades."

At the same time, many German business owners are reaching an age where they are thinking about selling their business, Albrecht-Mahmood underscored, pointing out that "there is often no successor within the family."
"This brings companies onto the market that might not have been available for sale a few years ago," he said.
Notable takeovers this year include ebm-papst, the Mulfingen-based manufacturer of electric motors and fans, which was bought by US company Madison Air for $5.4 billion in August.
In June, the long-established Augsburg-based company Everllence, formerly MAN Energy Solutions, was sold to Bain Capital, with the US investment firm acquiring a 51% stake in the company.
Fewer acquisitions, but more investments

According to Die Deutsche Wirtschaft (DDW), a German business information network focused on the Mittelstand (medium-sized and family-owned companies), no country owns more German firms than the United States. Of the total 7,861 companies identified in the database "German Companies Under Foreign Ownership," 1,750 are currently held by US investors.
Young startups — Germany's next tech champions?

PricewaterhouseCoopers (PwC), one of the world's leading auditing and consultancy organizations, also underscored the growing US investor interest in acquiring German companies. In a report, titled Destination Germany, PwC said that while the number of acquisitions and equity investments has not increased, the financial volume of the deals has jumped.
The report highlighted, in particular, the acquisition of BASF Coatings by the US investment firm Carlyle, in partnership with the Qatar Investment Authority (QIA), for around €7.7 billion.
The deal was struck on October 26, 2025, and closed on June 30 of this year.
Waiting for reforms

According to a recent survey by the American Chamber of Commerce in Germany, about 62% of the US companies active in the country are expecting business conditions to improve over the next three to four years.
Meanwhile, some 52% of them are planning to expand their operations in Germany, up from 49% in 2024.
Where are all of Germany's inventors?
At first glance, however, the increase in US acquisitions and equity investments does not seem to align with the decline in US investment flows to Germany last year.
According to the Bundesbank, significantly less investment capital flowed from the US to Germany in 2025 than in the previous year.

While foreign direct investment in Germany has risen overall — from €57.4 billion in 2024 to a total of €86.1 billion last year — investment from the US amounted to only €11.8 billion, nearly 44% less than in 2024.
In contrast, investment from the United Kingdom rose to around €26 billion.

"I would say the trend is continuing, although perhaps not simply in terms of higher deal numbers every year," Albrecht-Mahmood said. "The general interest in good German industrial companies, especially strong Mittelstand businesses, remains high."

Relatively low valuations also play a role, the expert argued. "Compared to the US, we still see situations where German companies are valued more moderately, particularly in the SME segment. This can make acquisitions quite attractive for international buyers."
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Lawmakers say budget increase for multi-purpose buildings 'based on needs'
articles.summary: House members on Tuesday described the increase in the allocation for multi-purpose buildings and local roads under the House-approved P7.2 trillion proposed budget for 2027 as "justified."

blocks.text: Published October 20, 2026 5:00pm

House members on Tuesday said the increase in the allocation for multi-purpose buildings and local roads under the House-approved P7.2 trillion proposed budget for 2027 was based on the needs of the public.

Representatives Terry Ridon of Bicol Saro party-list, Gerville Luistro of Batangas, and Joel Chua of Manila made the response after People’s Budget Coalition spokesperson AJ Montesa flagged the increase for multi-purpose buildings and local roads by as much as P170 billion.
The watchdog said that such an increase was reminiscent of flood control projects.
Ridon, however, said that the increase was based on the needs of the public.

“In any budget planning activity, it has to be needs based. We cannot compare various infrastructure projects as if they are the same. The very important, basic question is, are these line items [of projects] based on what the people need? Will this serve the common good?,” Ridon said in a press conference.

“If we talk about multipurpose buildings, these include senior citizens community centers, barangay and municipal facilities. So, this cannot be a general denial on the importance of these infrastructure projects. We cannot use generalities [in classifying infrastructure programs] when there are actual communities who will benefit from these projects, not just one or two people,” Ridon added.

Luistro said it is too early to judge the House version of the budget at this point when the Senate is yet to approve its own version and Congress yet to reconcile the differences of both chambers’ versions, if there are any.
“If there is an actual need for these projects, there is nothing wrong about that so long as it will serve the interest of the Filipino people,” Luistro said.
“What I take offense of are the ghost projects,” Luistro added.
Chua agreed, saying that allocation for multi-purpose buildings covers the need for evacuation centers too.

“If a multi-purpose structure is an evacuation center, is that prohibited? Clearly, evacuation centers are a constant need when we deal with climate change. We have to look at the merits of these kinds of [infrastructure] project,” Chua said. —VAL, GMA News

articles.title: Serbian prosecutor who investigated Belgrade Trump tower project ‘targeted with spyware’
articles.summary:
Apparent attempt to hack Rade Bajić’s iPhone comes amid efforts to undermine landmark criminal case

A Serbian prosecutor who investigated the authorities’ allegedly illegal scheme to help…

blocks.text: A Serbian prosecutor who investigated the authorities’ allegedly illegal scheme to help the Trumps build a tower in Belgrade has been targeted with advanced spyware, expert analysis indicates.

The finding suggests a disturbing new element in the authoritarian Serbian regime’s campaign to undermine what is believed to be the first criminal case related to global moneymaking drive of the US president’s family, which critics describe as a “pay to play” scheme trading the Trump administration’s favour for business opportunities.
Rade Bajić, the targeted prosecutor, said: “In my opinion, my involvement in this case was the sole reason for this unlawful spyware attack.”

Analysts at the Citizen Lab, a digital forensics laboratory, have not so far established who was behind the attack but the Serbian regime has previously been caught using spyware against its opponents.

blocks.caption: A screenshot from Trumpbelgrade.com shows the renderings of the proposed Belgrade development. Photograph: Trumpbelgrade.com

blocks.text: News of the alleged hack follows the Guardian’s revelations last week that Aleksandar Vučić, Serbia’s president, personally ordered that a cherished site in Belgrade be stripped of its legal protection so it could be handed over for a $500m Trump hotel and tower. Vučić, one of the Balkans’ most influential nationalists, hosted the US president’s son Donald Jr – “dear Don”, as he calls him – and son-in-law Jared Kushner as he ingratiated himself with the Trumps.

At the weekend, Vučić responded to the Guardian’s revelations about his role in the scandal by confirming details of a previously secret meeting. He indicated he had done nothing wrong. “I fought for my people,” he said. “And that’s what I’ll continue to do in the future.”

Last year prosecutors brought a landmark indictment against senior members of Vučić’s regime, accusing them of abusing their office to unlawfully strip the General Staff building – a monument to Serbia’s recent difficult history – of its protected status. They face years in jail if convicted.

Kushner, who was leading the Trump Belgrade development, called off the plans after the charges were made public. Vučić vowed reprisals, denouncing the prosecutors, including Bajić, a member of the specialised organised-crime unit that brought the indictment.

Bajić has said he was taken off the case without explanation shortly before the indictment was published. He went on to address one of the rolling protests against the regime triggered by widespread corruption, telling demonstrators in February: “The law will be equal for all.”

blocks.caption: Jared Kushner, left, was hosted in Belgrade by the then president, Aleksandar Vučić.  Photograph: Instagram/Aleksandar Vucic

blocks.text: In August, Bajić received a message from Apple saying it had “detected a targeted mercenary attack against your iPhone”.
Citizen Lab researchers, who have been analysing Bajić’s phone, said this was “a high confidence indicator that his device was likely targeted with mercenary spyware, such as Pegasus”.

Working with the Share Foundation, a Serbian rights group, they previously identified spyware attacks against anti-government protesters. In at least one case, the Citizen Lab analysts discovered Pegasus on a protester’s phone. “A zero-click infection with Pegasus spyware would not have been visible to the target, and would give the Pegasus attacker total access to the device,” they said of that discovery.

The Guardian’s Pegasus Project revealed how journalists, activists, politicians and others have been targeted by governments using the spyware. NSO Group, the Israel-based company that makes Pegasus, has been approached for comment.

blocks.caption: Aleksander Vučić, seen here with Donald Trump Jr, right, cannot run for a third presidential term so is attempting to become Serbia’s prime minister.  Photograph: Facebook/Aleksandar Vucic

blocks.text: Vučić, who stepped down late last month and called snap elections for 25 October, hoping to prolong his 12-year rule by switching from president to prime minister. He has been approached for comment, as has the prosecutors’ unit, which has said it may bring more charges in the General Staff building case.

articles.title: Brutal, revolutionary empire builder: Genghis Khan's legacy
articles.summary: As Berlin opens a major exhibition on the founder of the Mongol Empire and his successors, here's how Genghis Khan disrupted the course of history.

image.caption: A huge, highly revered golden statue of Genghis Khan is found in Mongolia's Chinggis Khaan National Museum, which opened in October 2022 Image: Chinggis Khaan National Museum

blocks.text: Genghis Khan is one of history's most radical figures. A blood-thirsty invader whose conquests caused the deaths of an estimated 40 million people, he was also a visionary political thinker who established the largest contiguous land empire in history.

The founder of the Mongolian Empire died in 1227. Ahead of the 800th anniversary of his death, Berlin's James-Simon-Galerie explores his legacy and the "Mongol Century" (1250–1350) in the exhibition "Genghis Khan and the World of the Mongols."
The power of a disruptive individual
The ruler remains "incredibly relevant" to this day, says Matthias Wemhoff, the director of the exhibition project.

"What the era of Genghis Khan — the 'Mongol century,' if you will — vividly demonstrates is how quickly established structures can collapse, how rapidly vast empires can vanish from the map and how swiftly the entire landscape can be utterly transformed," the archaologist tells DW.

The charismatic leader's unprecedented impact on the world also evokes present-day disruptive individuals who are triggering sudden, unpredictable societal shifts, says Wemhoff: "There's always been this question: Are world politics shaped by individuals or rather by groups and sociological processes?"

In this case, the answer is clear, says the museum director, who also co-wrote a 2026 book on the nomadic leader: "If Genghis Khan hadn't existed, the course of world history would truly have been entirely different — so much of it is inextricably linked to his person."

blocks.caption: Genghis Khan is revered in Mongolia as the founding father of the nation who united the warring steppe tribes. This statue is in the  Parliament Building in Ulan Bator Image: Mark Ralston/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: The founder of the world's largest empire

Genghis Khan was born as Temüjin around the year 1162. His father, a Mongol chieftain called Yesugei, died when he was still a child. His family was abandoned by its tribe. To secure his familial position, Temüjin killed his older half-brother, Bekter, when he was still a young teenager.
Thanks to his charismatic personality, he built alliances and found followers who helped him become the sole ruler on the Mongolian steppe. He formally adopted the title of Genghis Khan in 1206.

At its peak, the Mongol Empire covered approximately 24 million square kilometers (about 9.3 million square miles), stretching from China and Korea to parts of Eastern Europe and the Middle East, and accounting for over 16% of the Earth's total land area.

blocks.caption: Nomadic culture, with yurt tents, traditional costumes and music instruments is celebrated here in Mongolia's 'Mongols Nomadic Winter Festival'Image: AFP

blocks.text: Wemhoff lists various innovations under his rule: For one, Genghis Khan transformed warfare. Commanders were promoted for skill, discipline and loyalty rather than based on aristocratic rank or tribal loyalties. Soldiers were organized into decimal units of 10, 100, 1,000 and 10,000.

Despite being illiterate by modern standards, he also pushed for the introduction of the first written script for the Mongolian language, which allowed to build a state bureaucracy, track population and tax registers, record decrees, issue legal decisions and handle diplomacy.
A set of laws were established that replaced fragmented tribal customs with a unified legal system.
Trade was simplified through his adoption of a paper currency.
A policy of religious freedom was also established across the Mongol Empire, allowing all individuals to practice their chosen faith without state coercion.
Before the Mongol Empire, the Silk Road was fragmented by local conflicts and heavy taxes. Mongol rule placed the entire route under a single authority, making long-distance travel vastly safer.

blocks.caption: The 'paiza' acted as the world's earliest form of passport, granting official travelers protection and safe passage across EurasiaImage: Uuganbaatar Otgonbaatar/Chinggis Khaan National Museum, Ulaanbaatar

blocks.text: The Mongol Empire is known as a period of relative political stability, economic growth and cultural exchange, an era historians call the "Pax Mongolica."

But "it all came with incredible levels of cruelty. The millions of people who fell victim to the Mongols — the mass executions, the abuse of women — this happened on a scale previously unheard of," notes Wemhoff.
Shifting centers of power
The exhibition opens with a raid that happened after Genghis Khan's death, but took place just 260 kilometers (around 160 miles) away from Berlin: the 1241 Battle of Legnica, in Silesia, Poland.
It embodies the brutality and intensity of the Mongols' methods.

There came the "highly mobile, agile Mongols on small horses — lightly armored in lamellar gear, wearing helmets that left the face exposed, and wielding bows capable of firing 20 or more arrows in a single minute," points out Wemhoff.

European knights, heavily armored and mounted on large, massive warhorses, didn't stand a chance against their enemies. "When a hail of arrows rained down on them, the horses eventually went down, and the knights ended up lying on the ground, stuck on their back, much like a June bug," he adds. "The two styles of combat were simply mismatched."

blocks.caption: The Mongols also used deception to confuse and trap their opponentsImage: Staatsbibliothek zu Berlin – Preußischer Kulturbesitz, Orientabteilung, Diez A fol. 71 S. 58

blocks.text: The Mongols' Western campaigns shifted historic power centers in a way that still impacts world politics today.

For example, after the Mongol invasion of Kievan Rus', which was the first East Slavic state, its thriving capital Kyiv was reduced to a depopulated ruin. Moscow became a key regional power, partly because it chose to cooperate with the Mongols rather than pursue resistance.

"In our Western European collective memory, the Mongol invasion plays hardly any role. It's something of an anecdote," says Wemhoff, noting that the era of Genghis Khan and his immediate successors is barely mentioned in standard Western European school curricula.

Germans are mainly familiar with the name of the empire's founder through the 1979 Euro-disco pop band Dschingis Khan, which represented West Germany at the Eurovision Song Contest with a campy song of the same name that reduced complex history to extreme tropes.
But in eastern Europe, the Mongol invasions "changed everything fundamentally," says Wemhoff. "And so fundamentally that we that we still feel the consequences of it today."
The exhibition "Genghis Khan and the World of the Mongols" runs from October 21, 2026, to April 18, 2027.
Edited by Helen Whittle

articles.title: Apology can't be forced, Palace says in wake of Chinese envoy's remarks
articles.summary: It's difficult to force any one to apologize. Malacañang said this on Tuesday in the wake of Chinese Ambassador Jian Quan's remarks that China would easily win if it used force in the West Philippine…

blocks.text: Published October 20, 2026 4:56pm
It's difficult to force any one to apologize.

Malacañang said this on Tuesday in the wake of Chinese Ambassador Jing Quan's remarks that China would easily win if it used force in the West Philippine Sea, words that Philippine officials took as a threat amid the tensions in the region.
Philippine Coast Guard spokesperson Commodore Jay Tarriela said the envoy should apologize.
Asked about Tarriela’s comment, Castro said Foreign Affairs Secretary Maria Theresa Lazaro has already spoken to Jing Quan.

“Ang pagsasalita ng ‘sorry, I’m sorry’ hindi ito pinupuwersa, ito ay nanggagaling sa puso. So, tingnan natin na lang po natin kung ano ang magiging usapan ng representante ng China at ng ating representative sa katauhan po ni Secretary Tess Lazaro,” Castro said.
(Saying “sorry, I’m sorry’ cannot be forced, this comes from the heart. So we need to see how negotiations go with the Chinese representative and our representative Secretary Tess Lazaro.)
Castro said to let the talks between the two sides continue.
President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. has previously aired his concern over Jing Quan’s remarks, saying that it warranted a conversation between the two of them.
Asked if this discussion between Marcos and Quan will still push through, Castro said there was no information on the matter yet.

On Monday, Lazaro met with Jing Quan to convey the Philippines’ objection to his remarks, saying that such language aggravated the bilateral atmosphere and undermined both China and the Philippines’ efforts to build understanding.

"It is not the place of a foreign mission to publicly criticize or taunt Philippine officials and legislators who are acting within their mandates. As a democracy, the Philippines values freedom of expression and a plurality of voices, and it will not accept attempts by a foreign envoy to intimidate those who exercise them," the DFA said in a statement.
The relationship between China and the Philippines has grown tense over years of a maritime dispute over the West Philippine Sea.

Despite the Philippines winning its case over the flashpoint waters in the Permanent Court of Arbitration in 2016, China has continued to disregard the ruling and claim most of the West Philippine Sea for itself. —NB, GMA News

articles.title: Why Israeli Gen Z voters are drawn to the far right
articles.summary: More than half a million young people will cast their ballots in Israel next week - and they could make all the difference.

blocks.text: Far-right minister Ben Gvir (left) has significant support among Israeli youth
ByLucy Williamson
Middle East correspondentReporting fromJerusalem
When Israel's far-right National Security Minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, reached voting age, he was rejected from Israel's army for being too politically extreme.
His views have not changed much in the 30 years since then - but Israel has. Once shunned by the political establishment, he is now part of the government's inner sanctum of ministers.

On the campaign trail ahead of Israel's general elections next week, Ben Gvir is often surrounded by a jubilant pack of fresh-faced young fans, waving huge party flags over the heads of his numerous security guards.
At the covered market in Ramle - a mixed city of Jewish and Arab Israelis - he told us his message to young voters was to get out and vote.
"We see the support, we see the love [and] we want to win!" he said.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Nadav, 18, believes Ben Gvir is "trying to show that Israel is a strong country"

blocks.text: Nadav, 18, believes Ben Gvir is "trying to show that Israel is a strong country"
More than half a million first-time voters will cast their ballots in this election, which many Israelis see as existential for Israel's future security and identity.
Polls suggest it will be a tight race, and the new young voters could help decide the result.

More than 16% are planning to support far-right parties - either Ben Gvir's Jewish Power or the Religious Zionism party of his far-right ally Bezalel Smotrich - according to a poll for one of Israel's most popular newspapers, Yedioth Ahronoth.
And almost three-quarters see themselves as "right or centre-right", according to another survey for Israel's leading Channel 12 television network.
"Itamar Ben Gvir gives me a sense of security," said 20-year-old Mordechai, one of the young fans accompanying the politician to Ramle.
"Like everyone in history, from Trump to Moses, there are slips of the tongue that are a bit less good. So what? 90% of the things by Itamar are amazing."
"Itamar will give us safety, and when we go to the army, someone will have our backs and be behind us," said 18-year-old Nadav.
"I think he's trying to show that we're a strong country. For many years, we couldn't show we're strong in our beliefs. We couldn't express our ideology."

Meir Schreiber, an ultra-Orthodox 23-year-old who grew up in London, said the Hamas-led 7 October 2023 attacks on Israel, which triggered the Gaza war, also convinced him that Ben Gvir was the right choice.
"Young people understand that peace isn't something we can do," he told me, "because what happens to you when you're young shapes your personality - we saw October 7."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Polls suggest more than 16% of first-time voters are planning to support far-right parties next week

blocks.text: Polls suggest more than 16% of first-time voters are planning to support far-right parties next week

Ben Gvir is a divisive candidate in a divided nation: his political positions include annexation of the occupied West Bank, Jewish settlement of Gaza, and the "voluntary emigration" of Palestinians - positions and rhetoric that are widely condemned by liberal Israelis.

Several Western countries have imposed sanctions or travel bans on Ben Gvir and Smotrich for incitement against Palestinians. Both men are powerful ministers in Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's governing coalition.
As he and his entourage pushed their way between the stalls, some shopkeepers threw sweets; others, dark looks.
"I don't like him, he sows discord," one stallholder said. "Ramle is a mixed city - Jews and Arabs. There's no problem here, even after 7 October, but his message preys on young uneducated people."
The fact that he appears more popular with 18 to 22-year-olds than with their parents' generation is often put down, at least partly, to the impact of the 7 October attacks.
But political analyst Dahlia Scheindlin, who previously ran many Israeli political campaigns, said it was more than that.
"For about the last 20 years, we've seen young Israeli Jews are more right wing than average, and significantly more right-wing on many measures than the 55+ group," she told me.

"They have grown up under a series of wars with no personal experience of efforts to achieve peace. But for the most part, they have been socialised into the most extreme terms of the debate [as] legitimate to discuss: annexation, settlement expansion and - after 7 October - annexation of Gaza. And now they're voting for the first time."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Mordechai, 20, says Ben Gvir's "slips of the tongue" do not matter

blocks.text: Mordechai, 20, says Ben Gvir's "slips of the tongue" do not matter
A series of classroom debates filmed by Israeli satirist Lior Schleien recently highlighted the extreme views of some young Israelis.

The debates, in which he challenges racist or extreme views, drew a lot of attention in Israel, and included one exchange in which a student advocates killing all Arab citizens of Israel. That particular video has since been removed from Schleien's website.

Surveys suggest that first-time voters here are highly motivated to cast their ballots, with more than 80% saying they are likely to do so. But the same research suggests they are also more sceptical about democratic institutions and less engaged by political protests or petitions.
In a race that is largely deadlocked between two stable blocs of pro-government and anti-government supporters, getting new voters to the polling stations could make all the difference.
Opposition parties have been engaging younger voters with warnings about threats to democracy, new social media videos and younger candidates.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Polls show Benjamin Netanyahu and his coalition allies in a tight race with the opposition bloc

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
Polls show Benjamin Netanyahu and his coalition allies in a tight race with the opposition bloc

"In 2022 [in the last election], only 59% of the citizens living in Tel Aviv voted - in the most liberal city in the whole Middle East! In places where they voted for Ben Gvir, they voted at around 90%," said Yonatan Shalev, a 24-year-old candidate with the centre-right opposition party, Beyachad ("Together"), led by former prime minister Naftali Bennett.
He told me that Ben Gvir had understood the power of social media faster than other politicians.
"The liberal politicians didn't believe in TikTok, didn't believe in Instagram, and he took advantage of that arena."
Shalev said he had pushed his own party to reach young voters through social media.

"Three months ago, Ben Gvir was still the politician with the most amount of views on TikToks, the most amount of likes on TikTok, and Instagram as well," he explained. "Right now, Naftali Bennett is leading [that]."

His boss's Instagram page now features videos of the former prime minister lifting weights to rap music, or chatting with Shalev in the street. Even Netanyahu has joined in with a fast-paced militaristic social media video set to heavy beats.
"Younger people don't watch the news in Israel, [they] don't read the newspapers. The younger generation is getting all its details from TikTok and Instagram".

blocks.caption: Image caption, Beyachad candidate Yonatan Shalev says Ben Gvir understood social media's power sooner than others

blocks.text: Beyachad candidate Yonatan Shalev says Ben Gvir understood social media's power sooner than others
Yahlee Reske and Mika Magal, both 21 years old, rushed out of a nearby bar when they saw Shalev walk past.
"I love him," Mika told me.
"Yes," agreed Yahlee. "He's our age, he's so young and knows so much. It's hard to listen to people who are old and saying the same things over and over again."
Yahlee said she was doing national military service when the 7 October attacks unfolded.
"I don't think I ever looked at politics until then," she said. "But maybe if the government had been different on 7 October, things would have been better."

The same poll suggesting 16% of first-time voters would back a far-right party also suggested that Beyachad alone would take almost 9% of their votes, as would the centre-right Yashar party of Gadi Eisenkot.
At a student event in Tel Aviv last weekend, Ben Gvir was interrupted by protesters shouting, "Fascism will not pass", and forced off the stage.

Israel's young voters may be moving to the right, but they are still as divided as their country, over who they believe is the guardian of Israel's security and identity, and who is an existential threat.
Additional reporting by Morgan Gisholt Minard and Gidi Kleiman

articles.title: Supreme Court: COA audit not needed for Ombudsman to probe officials
articles.summary: The high court said COA and the Ombudsman exercise separate constitutional mandates, and one agency’s unfinished proceedings do not suspend the other’s work.

blocks.text: October 20, 2026 | 4:22pm
An undated photo of the Ombudsman office.
STAR / File

MANILA, Philippines — The Supreme Court has ruled that the Office of the Ombudsman has the authority to investigate public officials independently without waiting for the Commission on Audit (COA) to complete or finalize its audit proceedings involving the same transactions.

In the high court's decision dated April 22, the Supreme Court affirmed the administrative liability of several former Palawan provincial officials over procurement and project implementation irregularities tied to the province’s P2.572-billion share in the Malampaya Fund.

The case originated from four administrative complaints filed before the Ombudsman following a COA special audit into P966 million in allocated development funds intended for electrification, healthcare, education, and infrastructure projects in Palawan.
The Ombudsman found former Palawan provincial official Ronelo Del Socorro and several others administratively liable for grave misconduct, serious dishonesty, and gross neglect of duty.

Investigators uncovered multiple anomalies in the implementation of the provincial projects, including inadequate publication and posting of invitations to bid, improper evaluation of bidder eligibility, and the awarding of contracts despite incomplete documentation.

Additionally, the probe bared that identical personnel were assigned across multiple projects with overlapping execution schedules, while inaccurate accomplishment reports artificially overstated project progress to justify improper disbursements to private contractors.

The Ombudsman ordered the officials dismissed from government service, perpetually disqualified from holding public office, and stripped of their retirement benefits. The Court of Appeals subsequently affirmed the Ombudsman's ruling.

In their petition before the Supreme Court, the former officials argued that the Ombudsman’s investigation was premature because COA’s audit findings were not yet final, citing a subsequent COA decision ordering a review of certain projects to reassess liability.
Ruling
The Supreme Court rejected the argument, emphasizing that the Ombudsman and COA possess distinct and independent constitutional mandates.

Citing Article XI, Section 13(1) of the Constitution and Republic Act No. 6770 or the Ombudsman Act of 1989, the High Court explained that the Ombudsman is empowered to investigate any illegal, improper, or inefficient act of public officers on its own initiative or upon complaint.

“The Office of the Ombudsman is not required to wait for the finality of any audit or investigation by the COA before it can investigate unlawful and improper acts of public officials on its own,” the Supreme Court said.

The high court also warned that the Ombudsman’s investigatory mandate would be "severely diluted if the finality of a COA Audit Report would be considered as a suspensive condition before it could finally conduct an investigation.”

“Parties cannot compel the Office of the Ombudsman to accord weight to particular pieces of evidence of their choosing, nor may they dictate the manner by which an investigation is to be conducted,” the Supreme Court said.

Far-right AfD says emails stolen in September cyberattack

Germany's far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) said on Tuesday that it was looking into the theft and subsequent online publication of emails stolen by unidentified hackers during a cyberattack last month.
An AfD spokesperson said the hackers had targeted a hosting provider used by the party and appeared to have copied data from a small number of mostly inactive email accounts.
"The recent online publication of what is presumably a portion of this data is currently being investigated," the spokesperson said.
"A preliminary assessment can only be provided once this investigation has been concluded."
Although the spokesperson did not say how much data was stolen, an earlier report by the mass-circulation daily Bild put the number of AfD-linked emails published at more than 420,000.
According to Bild, the material published included not only emails sent by party figures such as co-leader Alice Weidel but also bank statements, academic certificates and membership lists.
The website hosting the material was offline by Tuesday afternoon.
However, archived versions showed a volume of 281 gigabytes of data under the headline "The party's own records, unedited."
The emails and other materials published have not yet been certified as authentic by any independent body.

The AfD, several state chapters of which have been classified as "confirmed right-wing extremist" by regional branches of Germany's domestic intelligence agency, has been topping recent national opinion polls and made gains in recent state elections.
Some politicians and civil society groups have called for it to be banned, arguing that the party is a threat to democracy, an accusation the party has rejected.

articles.title: Badenoch says Healey’s budget will be worse than Reeves’s if he doesn’t slash spending – UK politics live
articles.summary:
Conservative leader to give a speech later, while Treasury sources say Healey has ruled out a rise in capital gains tax

Here is Jessica Elgot’s story on John…

blocks.text: Key events

items: 1m agoBadenoch claims Labour's spending plans based on future 'fictional cuts' that won't happen
15m agoHealey to reject calls to raise capital gains tax in budget
42m agoBadenoch says Healey’s budget will be worse than Reeves’s if he doesn’t slash spending

blocks.text: Badenoch claims Labour's spending plans based on future 'fictional cuts' that won't happen

According to extracts from her speech briefed overnight, Kemi Badenoch will argue later that John Healey needs to slash spending in the budget because UK government borrowing costs are too high. She will say:

double quotation markBritain’s 30-year gilt yields are now above 6% - their highest level since 1998. That means every pound we borrow is already costing us £2 in less than 12 years. It is true the wars in Ukraine and Iran are pushing these rates up around the world. But they are no more Labour’s fault than they were ours when the war in Ukraine started. However, the UK is paying more to borrow than anyone else in the G7. We are paying over a percent more than Greece and Spain. We are paying nearly 2% more than Germany. The whole argument on defence spending would go away if our interest rates reduced. This is why we need to live within our means.
She will also argue that the spending reductions included in Labour’s plans for the final years of the decade are not credible.

double quotation markLast week the IMF praised the government for the work they were doing on reducing Britain’s deficit. They clearly don’t know the Labour party like we do. Labour’s deficit reduction plans to meet their fiscal rules are predicated on making huge cuts to the public sector in the final year of the spending period. I think there will be an election before then and they’ll never have to prove it. We are not fooled by made-up spending cuts, and neither it would seem are the IFS - who say relying on these projections would be a “work of fiction”. It would leave a £35bn black hole in departmental budgets. Labour have increased spending by more than £100bn in just two-and-a-bit years. They are not suddenly going to find some courage to cut spending in the final year of a parliament right before an election. Fictional cuts are not going to cut it. Investors simply aren’t buying it.
Healey to reject calls to raise capital gains tax in budget
Here is Jessica Elgot’s story on John Healey ruling out raising capital gains tax in the budget.
Badenoch says Healey’s budget will be worse than Reeves’s if he doesn’t slash spending
Good morning. John Healey, the chancellor, is delivering his first budget a week tomorrow, and this morning there are two news developments that will help to frame the way it is received.

The most important is on the front page of the Times, where Steven Swinford has a story firming up that has already been hinted that: that Healey has decided not to raise capital gains tax in the budget. This is significant because a capital gains tax hike was for a while seen as the government’s preferred money-raising ploy, not least because several senior figures in the cabinet were lobbying for one earlier this year. But now it is off the table, according to Swinford. He says:

double quotation markSenior allies of Andy Burnham, including several cabinet ministers, have been pressing for a rise in capital gains tax on the sale of second homes, shares and other assets to help repair the public finances. However, the chancellor has ruled this out after warnings that it could ultimately cost the government money if wealthy individuals left the UK or deferred selling assets … It means that the biggest “revenue raiser” in the budget will be a tax raid on banks, which will be used to help fund a targeted and temporary package of support on the cost of living. Healey will also reduce the government’s fiscal headroom — a buffer against future events — from £23bn to around £15bn.

There is a Whitehall myth about how the Treasury never gives out detail about what’s coming in the budget before it is actually announced. In fact, on certain issues, the Treasury regularly ensures that the media gets an accurate picture of what is coming in a budget to minimise the risk of the markets getting an unwelcome surprise. This is done not through on-the-record statements, but via murky background nods, winks and hints. That has been happening overnight, with journalists being assured that the Times’ story is accurate.

The second intervention is coming from Kemi Badenoch, the Conservative leader. In a speech this morning, she will claim that Healey’s budget will be even worse than the two delivered by Rachel Reeves, which raised taxes by £40bn and £26bn respectively. That is because Healey is not cutting spending, Badenoch will say. She will argue:

double quotation markJohn Healey is not Rachel Reeves. Many people see that as an improvement. How could it be worse than £70bn in new tax rises across just two budgets? However, I’m worried that next week John Healey will deliver a budget that does more damage to our country than either of Rachel Reeves’ budgets did. We are being told that next week’s budget is going to be “nothing to see here”. That is code in Whitehall for a budget that tries to do as little as possible … in the hope that no one notices. Picture the chancellor burying his head in the sand and hoping to deliver a budget so inconsequential that it “does no harm” - as some Labour MPs have been asking. But the problem is that Britain cannot afford to do as little as possible. Problems have caught up with us that we can no longer afford to run away from. First and foremost, that means living within our means.
The Tories have announced plans to cut government spending by £70bn a year. Badenoch thinks Healey should follow suit.
Here is the agenda for the day.
Morning: Andy Burnham chairs cabinet.
10am: Kemi Badenoch gives a speech and holds a press conference.
11.30am: Yvette Cooper, the health secretary, takes questions in the Commons.
Noon: Heather Hallett publishes the latest report from the Covid inquiry, covering care homes.
Noon: Downing Street holds a lobby briefing.
After 12.30pm: MPs resume their debate on the Northern Ireland Troubles bill.
2pm: Nigel Farage, the Reform UK leader, speaks at a rally in Plymouth.
